demand.reason: Global ruthenium consumption is estimated at roughly 30 metric tons annually, placing it securely within the negligible-demand band of ≤500 tons.

growth.reason: Demand is accelerating exponentially due to explosive requirements in AI data center hard-disk drives and sub-5nm logic chip interconnect liners, driving an aggressive high-growth trajectory (>12% CAGR).

supplier_concentration.reason:
Mining: South Africa dominates extraction, producing over 85% of primary global output from the UG2 reef, placing primary mining diversity at the highly concentrated maximum (Score 5).


Refining: Downstream refinement mirrors primary extraction. South Africa retains >85% of the processing baseline via integrated domestic metallurgical circuits (Score 5).

reserves.reason:
Time-frame: Global PGM resources represent centuries of supply. Against a micro-scale 30-ton annual extraction, the embedded ruthenium fraction is effectively limitless (>100 years).


Diversification: Total global reserves yield a calculated HHI of about 0.70, with South Africa holding about 83% of the PGM reserve base (63,000 of >76,000 tons). The geographic endowment matches the highly concentrated maximum score.

end_use.reason:
Defense & National Security (+1.5): functions as an irreplaceable electronics and hard-alloy component in defense infrastructure. Energy Generation & Grid (+1.5): serves as an essential co-catalyst in PEM electrolysers for green hydrogen synthesis. Advanced Semiconductors & Computing (+1.0): forms the critical magnetic recording layer in AI hard-disk drives and sub-5nm logic interconnects. Healthcare & Biomedical (+1.0): utilized widely across ocular brachytherapy plaques and clinical immunoassays. Construction & Heavy Industry (+0.5): acts as an essential catalyst for bulk ammonia and chemical manufacturing.


Sector presence scores total 5.5 across 5 qualifying sectors. The breadth bonus adds +2.0, yielding an objective composite score of 7.5.

substitutability_recyclability.reason:
Substitutability: No commercial drop-in substitute exists to replicate ruthenium's magnetic and electrical barrier properties in advanced chip architecture, necessitating fundamental system redesigns (Score 4).


Recyclability: Ruthenium is embedded in trace amounts in highly dispersive micro-electronics. End-of-life recovery is largely economically marginal, pacing secondary supply strictly in the low but non-trivial 5–20% recycling tier.

extraction_refining.reason: Ruthenium extraction requires identical processes to platinum: deep, hazardous shaft mining followed by smelting and highly complex, multi-stage hydrometallurgical separations, classifying it as a specialized chemical barrier.

upcoming_projects.reason: The project pipeline is adequate but tightly constrained as a co-product. Incremental expansions tied strictly to South African and Zimbabwean platinum asset developments are capable of adding 10–20% to supply within 3–5 years.

india_position.reason:
Import Dependence: India possesses zero commercial domestic extraction of ruthenium, rendering its growing electronics, medical, and data storage industries 100% import-dependent (Score 5).


Strategic Posture: Ruthenium is formally recognized on India's critical minerals list. Lacking binding KABIL overseas equity agreements, the posture remains at an early stage of declared strategic intent (Score 3).

price_volatility.reason: Ruthenium averaged $451–690/oz over 2021–2025 (USGS), then reached a record of about $1,750/oz in March 2026 (Johnson Matthey), roughly triple its level a year earlier, on demand from AI-driven data storage and falling South African output. A rise of more than 200% within five years meets the extreme band (Score 5).

capability.name: Ruthenium
capability.next_move: Grow recycling: secure spent catalysts and scrapped converters for Indian refiners, and assess the Boula-Nuasahi deposit.
capability.what_india_has: Hindustan Platinum (founded 1961) refines platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium and iridium from spent catalysts and says it is at peak production; Ravindra Heraeus recycles catalysts at Udaipur; Johnson Matthey (Manesar) and BASF (Chennai) coat autocatalysts in India; a Rs 1,500 crore recycling scheme covers catalytic converters. Resources of 20.92 t of platinum-group metals, 67% in Odisha.

stages.world: A by-product of platinum mining; South Africa has more than 85%.
stages.india: None. Boula-Nuasahi in Odisha is the only proven deposit.

stages.world: Smelters and precious-metal refineries beside the mines in South Africa and Russia; recyclers elsewhere.
stages.india: Hindustan Platinum and Ravindra Heraeus refine spent catalysts.
Hindustan Platinum also manufactures precious-metal products.

stages.world: Hard disks, chip resistors, chemical catalysts.
stages.india: Imported; 890 kg of iridium, osmium and ruthenium came in during 2022-23.

strategyList.name: Recycling (batteries, magnets, catalysts, PV)
strategyList.what: Shredding and hydrometallurgy of black mass; magnet recovery; spent-catalyst leaching; PV-panel recovery.
strategyList.outside_china: Battery recycling: China has over three-quarters of pre-treatment and 90% of material-recovery capacity; Europe, Japan, Korea and the US smaller.
strategyList.cost: India's scheme expects ~Rs 8,000 crore for 270+ kt/yr of capacity (~Rs 30 crore per kt/yr), yielding ~40 kt/yr of critical minerals.
strategyList.india_base: Lohum, Rubamin, the Bhopal magnet facility, CSIR-NML; Rs 1,500 crore incentive scheme (2025).

chemistryList.name: Catalysts and spent-catalyst recovery
chemistryList.who: Rubamin (Mo, Co, Ni from spent catalyst); Hindustan Platinum (PGM refining).
chemistryList.carries_over_to: Molybdenum and cobalt recovery; catalyst-grade chemicals.
chemistryList.summary: Spent catalysts are concentrated secondary sources of useful metals. India already has industrial experience recovering molybdenum and other metals, alongside precious-metal refining. The opportunity is to connect traceable waste collection, selective recovery and customer-approved products, while distinguishing regeneration from destruction and metal recovery.

links.how: Hindustan Platinum makes precious-metal catalysts and recovers platinum-group metals from used ones; it names platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium and iridium among the metals it refines.
